THE ATTACKER

Attacker knowledge is a least fixpoint

A Dolev–Yao attacker sees every message and can compute anything the primitives allow: hash what it knows, split concatenations, combine keys. The set of byte strings it can know is therefore the smallest set that contains what it observed and is closed under every computation it is allowed. DyLean defines it exactly like that, as a least fixpoint, and the two halves of that definition give the two kinds of proof: one shows an attack is possible, the other shows a secret is safe.

1 · The question

Secrecy theorems have the hypothesis k.AttackerKnows tr. To use it, we need a definition with two properties:

ClosedIf the attacker knows x, it knows hash x. If it knows a public key and a secret, it knows their DH. Every rule must be respected, otherwise attacks would be missed.
Nothing moreThe attacker must not "know" a random nonce it never saw. Without this, every secret would be known and no secrecy theorem would hold.

An inductive definition with one constructor per rule would give both. DyLean instead builds it from a generic fixpoint construction, because the rules come from many independent files, one per primitive, and must be combined after the fact.

2 · Least fixpoints, in 40 lines

DY/Misc/Fixpoint.lean states the Knaster–Tarski theorem for predicates. A set is a predicate, and a rule system is a function f from sets to sets: given what you already know, what can you derive in one step?

abbrev Set (α: Type u) := α → Prop

def IsMonotonic (f: Set α → Set α) : Prop :=
  ∀ set1 set2, (∀ x, set1 x → set2 x) → (∀ x, f set1 x → f set2 x)     -- knowing more never derives less

def mkLeastFixpoint (f: Set α → Set α) : Set α :=
  fun x => ∀ s: Set α, f s ⊆ s → s x       -- x is in every set closed under f

The definition is an intersection, not an induction: x is in the least fixpoint when x belongs to every set that is closed under f. Two theorems follow:

theorem mkLeastFixpoint_is_fixpoint (f) (h_mono: IsMonotonic f) : f (mkLeastFixpoint f) = mkLeastFixpoint f

theorem mkLeastFixpoint_is_least (f) (_: IsMonotonic f) (set: Set α) :
  (∀ x, f set x → set x) →                 -- if set is closed under f
  (∀ x, mkLeastFixpoint f x → set x)       -- then it contains the least fixpoint

Leastness is almost the definition itself; its monotonicity argument is not even used. The fixpoint property is the real Knaster–Tarski argument, and the only place monotonicity matters. Combining rule systems is a union: combine fs set x := ∃ id, fs id set x, monotone when each component is.

3 · Attacker rules

structure SubAttackerKnowledge (SubF: Type → Type) where
  pred: (Bytes → Prop) → Bytes → Prop
  pred_isMonotonic: DY.Fixpoint.IsMonotonic pred := by
    try simp [Fixpoint.IsMonotonic]
    try grind

pred p b reads: "if the attacker knows everything satisfying p, this rule lets it derive b". Each rule mentions p only positively, so the default tactic proves monotonicity and primitive authors never write it.

primitiverule: pred p out :=
Literal∃ lit, out = literalToBytes lit. No premise: every literal is known
Concat∃ lhs rhs, out = concat lhs rhs ∧ p lhs ∧ p rhs
∃ inp rhs i, some (out, rhs) = split inp i ∧ p inp, and the same for the right half
Hash∃ inp, out = hash inp ∧ p inp
DiffieHellman∃ sk, out = dhPk sk ∧ p sk · ∃ pk sk, out = dh pk sk ∧ p pk ∧ p sk
Signature∃ sk, out = vk sk ∧ p sk · ∃ sk nonce msg, out = sign sk nonce msg ∧ p sk ∧ p nonce ∧ p msg
RandomFalse. No rule produces random bytes

Each primitive file combines its rules, and the protocol's #combine … into attackerKnowledge combines the files into the global AttackerKnowledge: one rule system for all of Bytes.

4 · Base knowledge from the trace

Rules derive new bytes from known bytes; something has to be known to start with. Each entry kind says what it hands the attacker directly:

structure SubBaseAttackerKnowledge (ExecEntryT: Type) where
  attackerKnows: ExecTrace → ExecEntryT → Bytes → Prop      -- trace before, the entry, a byte string

def Trace.BaseAttackerKnows (tr: ExecTrace) (b: Bytes) : Prop :=
  match tr with
  | .nil => False
  | .snoc trBefore entry => BaseAttackerKnowledge.attackerKnows.attackerKnows trBefore entry b ∨ Trace.BaseAttackerKnows trBefore b

Only network messages contribute: attackerKnows _ entry msg := msg = entry.msg. Random records, events and stored states contribute False. A compromise does not leak through its own entry: the compromise action sends the state, and the attacker learns it as a message.

5 · The definition

def Bytes.AttackerKnows.baseKnowledge (tr: ExecTrace) : SubAttackerKnowledge BytesF :=
  SubAttackerKnowledge.fromPred tr.BaseAttackerKnows                  -- a "rule" with no premise

def Bytes.AttackerKnows.attackerKnowledge (tr: ExecTrace) : SubAttackerKnowledge BytesF :=
  SubAttackerKnowledge.combine' (fun (id: Fin 2) => match id with
    | 0 => AttackerKnowledge.attackerKnowledge                          -- the primitives' rules
    | 1 => baseKnowledge tr)                                            -- what the trace leaked

def Bytes.AttackerKnows (b: Bytes) (tr: ExecTrace) : Prop :=
  Fixpoint.mkLeastFixpoint ((Bytes.AttackerKnows.attackerKnowledge tr).pred) b

Unfolded: b.AttackerKnows tr holds when b belongs to every set s such that everything derivable in one step from s, or leaked by the trace, is in s. The trace enters only as a seed rule; the rules themselves never depend on the trace.

6 · Watching it grow

Because every rule has finitely many premises, the least fixpoint is also what you get by starting from nothing and applying all rules over and over. This widget does that for the two real runs, restricted to the terms that occur in each trace. Round 1 adds what the trace leaked, every literal, and the fields of every message; each later round adds whatever one rule application derives from what is already known. It stops when nothing new appears: that is the fixpoint, for this universe of terms.

Known after this round
Never derived

The widget runs in your browser on the exported terms. It illustrates the definition; it is not the Lean proof, and it only considers terms that appear in the trace, which is enough to show which secrets stay out.

7 · Two directions, two kinds of proof

The doc comment on SubAttackerKnowledge.Implies says it plainly:

"The attacker knowledge AttackerKnows is the weakest predicate P such that every sub-attacker knowledge predicate att, att.pred P b implies P b. The attacker knowledge satisfies this property: this is the theorem Bytes.AttackerKnows.prove. The attacker knowledge is the weakest predicate: this is the theorem Bytes.AttackerKnows.is_least_fixpoint."

Closure: proving an attack

theorem Bytes.AttackerKnows.prove (att: SubAttackerKnowledge SubF) [AttackerKnowledge.Has att] (b tr) :
  att.pred (Bytes.AttackerKnows · tr) b → Bytes.AttackerKnows b tr          -- one rule, applied to known premises
theorem Bytes.AttackerKnows.prove_from_base : tr.BaseAttackerKnows b → Bytes.AttackerKnows b tr

Each primitive wraps prove into a friendly lemma such as attacker_knows_hash : inp.AttackerKnows tr → (hash inp).AttackerKnows tr. The compromise sanity check uses them to show the attacker really can compute the session key, which the attacker's network step requires before it may send it:

k = hash (dh yPk xSk) attacker_knows_hash └─ dh yPk xSk attacker_knows_dh ├─ yPk field of the message at index 12 MessageSentAt_implies_AttackerKnows, split └─ xSk field of the message at index 16 MessageSentAt_implies_AttackerKnows, split (sent by compromise of the state at 6)

Leastness: proving security

theorem Bytes.AttackerKnows.is_least_fixpoint (pred: Bytes → Prop) (b tr)
  (pf1: SubAttackerKnowledge.Implies AttackerKnowledge.attackerKnowledge pred)      -- pred is closed under the rules
  (pf2: SubAttackerKnowledge.Implies (Bytes.AttackerKnows.baseKnowledge tr) pred)   -- pred contains the leaks
  : Bytes.AttackerKnows b tr → pred b

This is an induction principle: to show every known byte string satisfies some property, show the property is closed under each rule and holds for everything leaked. The security theorem picks "publishable":

theorem Bytes.AttackerKnows_implies_Publishable (b) (tr: ProofTrace) :
    tr.Invariant → Bytes.AttackerKnows b tr.erase → b.Publishable tr := by
  intro h_tr
  apply Bytes.AttackerKnows.is_least_fixpoint (·.Publishable tr) b tr.erase
  · intro b; exact inst.inst.pf b tr h_tr                  -- every primitive's rules preserve Publishable
  · intro b                                                -- everything leaked is Publishable
    simp only [AttackerKnows.baseKnowledge, SubAttackerKnowledge.fromPred]
    apply Trace.BaseAttackerKnows_implies_Publishable
    assumption
  • Rules preserve publishability. Each primitive proves SubAttackerKnowledgeTheorem: if the inputs of its rule are publishable, so is the output. For hash it is three lines, because a hash has its input's label and validity. These instances combine automatically.
  • Leaks are publishable. BaseAttackerKnows_implies_Publishable is an ordinary induction on the trace: a leaked byte string came from a message entry, and a message entry's invariant is exactly that its content is publishable.

Then "publishable" means "label is corrupt", and every secrecy argument in DyLean starts from there, as the labels page explains.

8 · Why least, not greatest

Closure alone would also be satisfied by "the attacker knows everything", which is closed under every rule. Leastness rules that out, and the induction principle above is precisely what leastness buys.

A greatest fixpoint would be disastrous here, and the split rules show why. Every byte string b is the left half of concat b x, by split_concat. So the set of all bytes is consistent with the rules in the backwards direction: each of its members is derivable in one step from a member. The greatest fixpoint would contain every random nonce, justified circularly. The least fixpoint contains only what has a finite derivation from the trace. This argument is ours, not stated in the code, but it follows directly from the rules.

9 · Modularity

  • Rules are separate from the trace. AttackerKnowledge is fixed per protocol and mentions no trace; the trace only adds the seed rule.
  • Rules combine by union. combine over primitives is a union of rule systems, and closure of a union is closure under each part, so each primitive's closure proof stands alone.
  • Knowledge only grows. AttackerKnows_le: if the attacker knows b on a trace, it knows b on every extension. Its proof is itself an application of leastness.
  • The attacker's actions are gated by it. The attacker's network step has precondition b.AttackerKnows tr, and its Hoare triple is discharged by AttackerKnows_implies_Publishable. So reachable traces contain only messages the attacker could compute.
The prose and the iteration widget are editorial; the cards are the compiler's view of ../dylean; the terms come from the exported runs.
